summary: Discusses how national bibliography numbers, assigned by national libraries, can be supported within the URN framework. It was replaced by RFC 8458.

eli5.summary: It turns a library's book number into a permanent online name.

questions: what is a national bibliography number
how do i use nbn as urn
subtitle: Turning library catalog numbers into permanent global identifiers for online documents.

tldr.problem: National libraries assign unique catalog numbers to documents, but these numbers are only unique within each country and cannot be used globally to identify online resources.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3188 describes how to augment national bibliography numbers (NBNs) with a country code prefix to create globally unique Uniform Resource Names (URNs) that work within the URN framework defined in RFC 2141.
tldr.outcome: Libraries worldwide can now use NBN-based URNs to persistently identify electronic documents in their Web archives and catalogs. This RFC was superseded by RFC 8458.

today: RFC 3188 is an Informational document that was obsoleted by RFC 8458 in September 2018. It described how to use national bibliography numbers as URNs for persistent identification of electronic documents in Web archives.

sections.title: National Bibliography Numbers as Global Identifiers
sections.content:
RFC 3188 shows how national bibliography numbers (NBNs)—persistent identifiers assigned by national libraries—can be used as Uniform Resource Names (URNs) in the global Internet naming system. NBNs have been used for centuries to identify printed materials; the RFC extends this practice to electronic documents.

National libraries including Finland, Norway, and Sweden have already begun assigning NBN-based URNs to electronic resources and harvesting Web documents for long-term preservation. The RFC provides a formal specification for using NBNs as URNs according to the URN framework in RFC 2141.
sections.eli5: Old libraries have always given each book a number. Now we can add a country code to that number to make it work on the Internet.

sections.title: What Are National Bibliography Numbers
sections.content:
National Bibliography Numbers are identifiers assigned only by national libraries for documents that lack a publisher-assigned identifier (like ISBN) but are cataloged in the national bibliography. Each national library maintains its own independent NBN system; there is no global authority controlling them.

NBNs serve as a fallback mechanism: if a document cannot be given an ISBN, ISSN, or SICI (Serials Item and Contribution Identifier), it receives an NBN. Syntax and scope vary by country. Finland's F-codes, for example, have been used since the early 20th century. Web harvesting applications like NEDLIB use MD5 checksums to generate NBNs for archived Web documents automatically.
sections.eli5: A national bibliography number is what your country's library gives to a book or document when nobody else has already given it a number.

sections.title: NBN URN Format and Encoding
sections.content:
To create a globally unique NBN-based URN, the NBN string is prefixed with a two-letter ISO 3166 country code or other registered prefix, separated by a hyphen. The general model is urn:nbn:<country-code>-<NBN-string>. For example, urn:nbn:fi-fe19981001 is a Finnish URN with an F-code.

When a country has multiple national libraries or trusted organizations, colon-separated sub-namespace codes can be used. For instance, urn:nbn:fi:st:<string> is a Statistics Finland sub-namespace. Non-ISO prefixes must be registered globally with the Library of Congress. NBNs consisting of alphanumeric characters require no special encoding when used as URNs.
sections.eli5: The URN looks like this: urn:nbn:XX-YYYYY, where XX is your country code and YYYYY is the library's number.

sections.title: Resolution and Storage
sections.content:
The country code prefix guides users to the appropriate resolution service. National bibliography databases (or Web archives maintained by libraries) store the actual documents and metadata. When an NBN-based URN is resolved, the system typically returns bibliographic information including URLs to both the document in the Internet and a copy in the national library's legal deposit collection.

Web harvesting applications may be unable to deliver electronic materials outside the library's premises due to legal deposit restrictions. In such cases, the resolution service returns metadata and information about where the physical resource is stored.
sections.eli5: When someone looks up your NBN URN on the Internet, the system uses the country code to find the right library's catalog, and then shows the document or information about it.

sections.title: Persistence and Uniqueness
sections.content:
NBN-based URNs are persistent because they rely on the stability of national libraries and their bibliographic systems, which have existed for decades. NBNs are unique at the national level only; the country code prefix ensures global uniqueness.

When identifier assignment is automatic (using MD5 checksums, for instance), an NBN-based URN resolves to a single instance of a work. The likelihood of two different documents sharing the same MD5 checksum is approximately 2^-64. Manual assignment by library catalogers follows national guidelines that determine whether different versions of a work receive the same or different NBNs.
sections.eli5: These numbers stay the same forever because libraries don't go away, and two different documents almost never get the same number.

sections.title: URN Namespace Registration
sections.content: RFC 3188 includes a formal registration for the NBN namespace ID with the IETF. The NBN namespace has been in production use since summer 1998, with thousands of URNs delivered in Finland, Sweden, and Norway. Non-ISO prefixes must be registered with the Library of Congress at nbn.register@loc.gov.us. Sub-namespace codes must be registered by the assigning national library and made available via the Web.
sections.eli5: This document officially registers NBN as a valid URN type with IETF, meaning the internet recognizes it as a legitimate way to name things.
